Selling in Louisville

Louisville and Jefferson County merged their governments on January 6, 2003, and Louisville Metro now covers the whole county. Smaller cities such as Shively still exist inside it with limited powers. Louisville is also the only first-class city in Kentucky, a legal category that affects some local revenue and public safety rules. The July 1, 2025 population estimate is 641,962.

A seller deals with one metro government for permits and code questions, but the housing stock is very uneven: Victorian mansions, post-war brick ranches, river-bottom shotgun houses and subdivisions built since the interstates opened. Old Louisville is the largest Victorian preservation district in the country, and the Bardstown Road and Frankfort Avenue corridors have drawn renovation money since the 1980s. West End, South End and East End are the three informal sides of town, and prices and housing types differ among them.

Floodplain and flood history

Much of Louisville sits on a wide, flat floodplain that was once swampland and had to be drained as the city grew. In January 1937 the Ohio River crested at 57.15 feet, almost 30 feet above flood stage, and 60 to 70 percent of the city went under water. Land east of Interstate 65 sits above the floodplain on gently rolling hills, and the far south of the county reaches the Knobs.

If your house is west or north of that line, expect a buyer to ask about flood zone status, sump pumps and past water in the basement. Keep records of any water damage and repairs. Insurers and lenders ask the same questions, and a house with water history can complicate financing.

Jobs and commutes

Louisville's economy runs on moving freight. UPS operates its Worldport air hub at Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport, and the city sits at the crossing of Interstates 64, 65 and 71, ringed by the I-264 and I-265 beltways, plus two major freight railroads. Two Ford plants and GE Appliances anchor manufacturing, and Brown-Forman is headquartered in the city.

These jobs sit in different parts of the county, so the commute from a given neighborhood varies. Average travel time to work is 22.5 minutes. Look at recent sales on your own street instead of relying on a county-wide figure.

Owners who carry a mortgage pay a median $1,555 a month, against $1,120 for rent. Churchill Downs, the University of Louisville, Bellarmine and Spalding universities, and the parks system add to housing demand in different neighborhoods. Waterfront Park runs along the Ohio River near downtown, and the Parklands of Floyds Fork spreads across eastern Jefferson County.

Rentals and vacant houses

Owners of long-term rentals must register under Chapter 119 of the Metro Code of Ordinances, and Metro's rental registry lets you search registered properties by street name. If you are selling a rental, check that its registration is current before closing. Registration questions go to Codes and Regulations at (502) 574-2508.

  • Short-term rentals apply through the Metro Business Portal.
  • Vacant and abandoned houses draw attention from Code Enforcement. In a pilot area north of Market Street between 18th and 26th streets, Metro secured 53 vacant properties with clear boarding.
  • Building, fence, wrecking and residential alteration permits are all handled through the Metro Business Portal, and Metro311 takes complaints by phone, app or email.

A house with open permits or code cases is harder to list, which is one reason sellers turn to cash buyers. Look up your case in the Metro portal to see what is outstanding, and tell the buyer about any violation notices.

Recording a deed in Jefferson County

The Jefferson County Clerk records deeds for property inside the county. Its checklist asks for:

  • The preparer's name, address and signature.
  • A source of title by book and page, and a full legal description.
  • Complete grantor and grantee addresses, fair market value and a mailing address for the tax bill.

A deed that claims no transfer tax is owed must cite the statute that says so. For deeds that do owe it, KRS 142.050 sets the tax at $0.50 per $500 of declared value, payable by the seller, with partial units rounded up. The Jefferson County PVA site searches by address or parcel ID and takes homestead filings. Your closing agent can say how this year's property tax will be divided.

Cash offers for older houses

A cash offer fits when condition, paperwork or timing blocks a regular sale. Louisville has many older houses, from Victorian-era buildings in Old Louisville to mid-century brick in the South End, and the repairs a lender would insist on can be costly. Cash suits:

  • An inherited house whose family lives outside Kentucky and whose contents are still inside.
  • A long-term rental never registered, or one with an open Codes and Regulations case.
  • A vacant house that has attracted break-ins.
  • A floodplain house with water history that complicates insurance and financing.

Ask for the offer in writing, obtain payoff figures from the title company, and compare the net with a listing after repairs, carrying costs and transfer tax.

Before you list

Make a short file for the buyer. Include the flood and water history, if any, the permit records for past work, and the rental registration if the house has been a long-term rental. Ask Metro whether any open permit or code case is attached to the address, since a title search will find it. If the house is vacant, secure it, because an empty property draws attention from Code Enforcement and from break-ins.

Then decide how much repair makes sense. Older houses often need wiring, plumbing or foundation work that a lender's appraiser will flag. Collect bids so you can weigh them against the discount a cash buyer will ask for.

What closing involves

The title company searches the Jefferson County records for the mortgage and any lien. Each one is paid from your proceeds at closing. You sign the deed, the transfer tax is paid to the clerk, and the deed is recorded. Request the payoff letter from your lender before you list so the figure is ready when offers arrive.

Is Louisville the same as Jefferson County?

Yes for governing purposes. Since the 2003 merger, Louisville Metro covers the entire county, though smaller cities inside it keep limited powers of their own.

Do I have to register a Louisville rental before selling it?

Long-term rentals must be registered under Chapter 119 of the Metro Code. Check your listing on the registry by street name before you sell, and call Codes and Regulations at (502) 574-2508 if it shows a problem.

What is the transfer tax on a Louisville sale?

The seller pays $0.50 per $500 of value under KRS 142.050, with any partial unit rounded up. The county clerk collects it at recording.

Does it matter whether my Louisville house is east or west of I-65?

It can. The land west of I-65 is mostly on the old Ohio River floodplain, while the east side is above it. Buyers and insurers ask about flood history, so keep your records of any water damage and repairs.

Yes, open code issues do not bar a sale. Look up the case in the Metro portal to see what is outstanding, and tell the buyer about any violation notices.

Selling fast in Lexington

Lexington is a city and a county in one. The city limits match Fayette County, and the two governments have been merged since 1974. The 2020 count was 322,570 people, and the estimate for July 1, 2025 is 329,751. There are 139,715 households, the median owner-occupied value is $293,500, and 53.8% of homes are owner-occupied.

That leaves almost half of households as tenants. Landlords and small investors are regular purchasers, and one who pays cash can skip the appraisal and repair demands that slow a bank-financed deal on a tired, tenanted or estate-held property.

The urban service area

Lexington drew a line around itself early. In 1958 the city adopted an urban service area, described as the first urban growth boundary in the country, and kept a 40-acre minimum for land outside it so the horse farms stayed whole. The line was widened by 5,300 acres in 1996, which is why newer subdivisions sit on the edge of a city that is still about 285 square miles in total.

Zoning outside the boundary differs from zoning inside it. If your house is near the edge, call the Division of Planning to learn which side it is on before you name a price.

Who buys a Lexington house

Lexington is a college town with a professional workforce. The University of Kentucky is the largest employer, with 16,743 employees in 2020, and Fayette County Public Schools and the area's hospitals add thousands more. Median household income is $69,479. Buyers include university staff, hospital workers, people in the horse industry who work around Keeneland and the Kentucky Horse Park, and investors who rent to students. Transylvania University and Bluegrass Community and Technical College add to rental demand.

About 79.8% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so roughly one in five had moved. The metro area of 516,811 people also takes in Clark, Jessamine, Bourbon, Woodford and Scott counties, and many buyers arrive from those neighbors. I-75 skirts the city limits and I-64 passes along the north.

Deed tax and recording

The same office prepares the county's property tax bills, so one stop can answer questions on the deed, the bill's mailing address and any lien releases. Its old land records help when a family house needs its chain of title traced.

Property tax when you sell mid-year

Fayette County prices each parcel as it stood on January 1, then applies rates set by the urban county government, the school district, the state and other taxing bodies. Payment is due by December 31, and late payment carries heavy penalties.

The bill carries the January 1 owner's name. When a sale happens after that date, the bill is mailed in care of the buyer, though a closing right before printing can miss the update. Splitting the year between buyer and seller happens at the closing table, so ask your closing agent or attorney for the proration worksheet.

Homestead exemption and appeals

Homeowners aged 65 or over, and those on disability payments, can apply to the PVA for the Homestead Exemption. A 2026 assessment you disagree with can be reviewed on request, but the finalized figure stays on this year's bill. The PVA site also offers a tax calculator and a mailing address change form, which a departing owner should file so later notices reach the right person.

Roughly 46 percent of local households rent, so buyers used to tenanted houses are not hard to find. Gather the lease, the deposit ledger and the tenant's contact details before you list. How a Lexington closing runs

After you accept an offer, the closing agent or attorney runs a title search through the Fayette County Clerk's land records. A mortgage, a contractor's claim or an old lien will appear there and has to be paid or released from your proceeds. Order a payoff letter from your lender early, since it sets the exact amount owed on the closing date.

At the table you sign the deed, the transfer tax is paid, and the clerk records it. A cash buyer needs no lender appraisal, so the date is often yours to choose. When the buyer is financed, allow time for the appraisal and loan approval, and expect a request for repairs if the appraiser flags defects.

Selling a house in Bowling Green

Warren County's seat is a college-and-factory city on the Barren River, third in Kentucky after Louisville and Lexington. The July 2025 estimate is 78,505 people, up 8.6 percent from 2020. Interstate 65 runs through town between Louisville and Nashville, Interstate 165 heads north to Owensboro, and US 31W, US 231 and US 68/KY 80 cross it as well.

Only 36.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so this is a renter's city, and a house here is often sold to an investor or landlord as readily as to a family. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $241,900. Median gross rent is $998 a month, and median owner costs are $1,447 with a mortgage and $553 without. The 2020 census counted 31,797 housing units, with 11.4 percent vacant and a rental vacancy rate of 11.5 percent. With rental vacancy above 11 percent, a house listed as a rental can sit empty between leases, which is worth weighing if you own one.

City and school tax rates by location

Two collectors send bills here. The city's Treasury office bills for the city and for the Bowling Green Independent School System, and the Warren County Sheriff sends the county bill. The city mails roughly 23,000 bills each October, due in full by December 31. Unpaid city taxes can face a foreclosure action filed six months after the due date. The rates below are per $100.

City proper adds a 0.2030 city rate and an 0.8420 city school rate to the county's 0.2145 and the state's 0.1030. Check the Finance page for the rate in force when you sell.

Which school district is a house in?

The answer depends on the street. Bowling Green Independent serves the inner city, and Warren County Public Schools has the outlying sections. An "annex" of homes inside city limits attends county schools, and the school tax rate differs between the two. Tell buyers which district applies, since it moves the tax figure.

Paying the county bill and closing

The Warren County Sheriff prefers a check or money order mailed to P.O. Box 807, Bowling Green, KY 42102, or delivered to 1347 KY-185, Suite 1. The office answers at (270) 842-1633. Online card payments carry a $1.50 fee up to $60 and 2.49 percent above that. Partial payments are not accepted on a current-year bill.

  • 2 percent discount from October 1 through November 1, face value from November 2 through December 31, a 5 percent penalty in January and 21 percent from February 1 through April 15.
  • Kentucky law issues the bill in the name of the January 1 owner. If you sold, forward the bill to the buyer.
  • A closing agent or attorney usually prorates the year between buyer and seller, but the sheriff needs the full bill paid by one or both of them.

For a delinquent prior year, call the Warren County Clerk at (270) 842-9416 for the payoff.

Homestead exemption

Owners 65 or older, and owners who are totally disabled, can apply for the homestead and disability exemptions at the PVA, (270) 843-3268. Apply before you list if you qualify, because a buyer has to file again on their own.

What happens to unpaid tax bills

After April 15 an unpaid bill becomes a certificate of delinquency, recorded as a lien under KRS 134.122, and the County Attorney reports 12 percent annual interest under KRS 134.125. If the certificate stays unpaid 90 days, third-party purchasers may buy it. A certificate cannot be sold while the owner has a payment agreement with the County Attorney, whose office offers plans running 4 to 8 months at (270) 782-2760. If a purchaser already bought the certificate, you deal with that purchaser instead. The clerk's sale takes place each summer at 429 E 10th Ave, Suite 100.

City permits and short-term rentals

The Building and Inspection Division at 707 E Main Ave, reachable at 270-393-3615 or 270-393-3676 on weekdays from 8 am to 4 pm, issues permits. A building permit is required to construct, enlarge, alter, repair or demolish, or to change a building's use. The fee is $20 up to $3,000 of work, then $2.50 per $1,000 above that up to $500,000. All fences need a permit, and an accessory structure under 200 square feet falls under a no-fee permit. A certificate of occupancy costs $3 after a final inspection.

Converting a house to a short-term rental counts as a change of use. It needs inspections and a $45 Short Term Rental Permit. If you are selling a house that someone else operates that way, ask for the permit paperwork. No permit is needed just to sell, but close out any open permit work before you list.

Selling a rental or a house with tenants

Because renters fill most of the housing here, many sellers own a rental. Tell the buyer's side early whether the house is occupied, when the lease ends and whether the tenant pays on time. Hand over the lease and the deposit records, and ask the closing agent to credit the deposit at the table. A house that has been a short-term rental should come with its permit paperwork, since the city permit is tied to the operator and not the property.

If a vacant rental needs work between leases, a direct cash buyer may suit you better than a listing, because the buyer does not need the house to pass a lender's appraisal and you avoid carrying another month of costs while it sits empty.

Steps before accepting an offer

  2. Check the sheriff's bill and the city bill, and ask the clerk about any earlier year.
  3. Gather permit papers for any recent work and rental permits if relevant.
  4. Get a mortgage payoff letter close to the planned closing date.
  5. Agree in the contract who pays the year's tax and who covers repairs.

A cash buyer takes the house as it stands, so repairs and a lien paid from proceeds do not hold up the sale the way they can with a lender. Whichever route you choose, keep copies of the bills, payoff letters and permits in one folder, and ask the closing agent for a settlement statement ahead of time so every charge makes sense before you sign.

Property maintenance code

The city enforces a Property Maintenance Code through Public Works.   • Code Enforcement Officers investigate, inspect and document conditions on a property.

The bills are available by November 1 and due by December 31, and payments received before November 30 get a 2% discount. After the due date a 10% penalty plus interest applies.

Is an inspection required before a Frankfort tenant moves in?

Yes. A rental inspection is required before any new tenant takes possession, and the fee is $20, or $100 if the unit has no current inspection. Call Planning and Building at 502-352-2094 to schedule it.

Are short-term rentals allowed in Frankfort?

Yes, with limits. Each unit pays a $250 annual license fee, and non-owner-occupied rentals in the Special Capital and Special Historic districts are conditional uses with caps. Owner-occupied rentals must meet the ordinance's standards for stay length, occupancy and parking.

Does floodplain location matter when selling in Frankfort?

It changes what you can build or remodel, because construction there needs a local Floodplain Development Permit and elevation certificate review. Planning and Community Development can say whether one is on file for your address.

Selling in Henderson

Henderson sits on a bluff above the Ohio River in north-central Henderson County, about 10 miles south of Evansville, Indiana, and 30 miles west of Owensboro. The July 2025 estimate is 27,822 residents, a little under the 2020 figure of 27,981. The slow dip means most buyers are local households or people who commute across the river.

As county seat, Henderson funnels deeds, tax bills and court filings through the same few downtown blocks. A house with clean title and no open city orders closes quickly. An estate still in probate, an unpaid weed lien or a back tax bill drags things out, so clear those first.

Prices, rents and who owns

The middle of the owner-occupied range is $160,100. Owners with a mortgage spend a median $1,253 a month on housing, owners without one spend $494, and renters pay a median $771. Only 54.1% of households own, so rentals are a big slice of the housing stock. There are 12,341 households, averaging 2.18 people, and median household income is $48,186.

Adults 65 and older are 18.8% of residents, a group that often ends up selling an inherited or long-held home. At these price points, repair bills weigh heavily on the final number. A roof and furnace job can swallow a large share of the sale price, so owners with deferred maintenance often compare an as-is sale with paying contractors first. Gather two or three quotes before you decide.

Older neighborhoods

Henderson began as a river landing called Red Banks and was laid out in 1797 with unusually wide streets. Dark tobacco drove the economy for generations. Older residential areas such as Audubon, Weaverton and the former East End grew up around that industry, and many houses there date from the early 1900s. Expect a buyer's inspector to look hard at wiring, plumbing and foundations in a house that age.

The climate is humid and warm, so inspectors also check roof age, attic airflow and cooling equipment. Write down the age of each system before the first showing.

US 41 crosses the Bi-State Vietnam Gold Star Bridges to Evansville and runs south toward Madisonville and Hopkinsville. I-69 in Kentucky ends at the US 41 and US 60 interchange at Henderson. Local industry includes aluminum, automotive and appliance parts, plastic injection molding, tool and die work and food processing. Code violations and city liens

Since July 1, 2017, a Code Enforcement Board has handled property maintenance and nuisance cases. Final orders are posted by the city, and registered lienholders get a monthly email notice. Typical entries are weeds, rubbish, clutter and inoperable vehicles.

  • A lienholder of record has 45 days from the emailed notice to fix the violation or pay the fines and abatement charges.

Property tax and deed tax at closing

Real estate bills come from the Sheriff's Office in late October or early November and are payable starting November 1. A bill still open on the January 1 after its due date is delinquent. The Sheriff then passes it to the County Clerk, where interest runs at 1% a month on top of penalties, and the property stays encumbered until the bill is paid in full.

The person giving the deed pays a state deed tax of 50 cents per $500 of declared value, rounded up (KRS 142.050). The clerk collects it at the counter before the deed is recorded. Foreclosure sales and voluntary surrenders in place of foreclosure fall outside the tax, as do gifts between parent and child for nominal money.

The closing statement usually bills the seller for the months of the tax year already owned. Ask the Sheriff's Office for a current figure so the statement matches the bill.

Selling a rental or short-term rental

Yes, you can sell one, though zoning limits what a buyer may do with it. Land use is set in Appendix A of the city's Code of Ordinances, and Code Enforcement explains setbacks, allowed uses and parking. In April 2024 the Board of Commissioners took up an ordinance amending that appendix for short-term rental property, which touches several residential, business and riverfront districts. Check with Code Enforcement on your parcel before you advertise the house as a short-term rental.

When tenants occupy the house, collect the lease and the deposit ledger early, since buyers ask when the term ends.

How a Henderson closing runs

After a contract is signed, the closing agent searches title at the County Clerk's office. Open tax bills, code liens and any mortgage show up in that search, and each is paid from your proceeds. That is why a payoff letter from the lender, a tax figure from the Sheriff and a code file from the city are worth requesting before you list.

A cash purchase skips the appraisal and lender review, so the closing day is set by agreement. A conventional sale adds showings, an appraisal and loan approval. Either way, you sign the deed, pay the deed tax at the clerk's counter, and the deed is recorded.

Fast-sale routes

It depends on the route. A cash purchase closes on an agreed date, and a conventional sale adds showings, an appraisal and loan approval. Either way the deed is recorded at the Henderson County Clerk, after open code orders and tax bills are paid off.

Who pays the deed transfer tax in Henderson County?

The seller pays it, since the tax falls on the grantor named in the deed. KRS 142.050 sets the rate at $0.50 per $500, and the clerk collects before recording. Foreclosure transfers are exempt.

What if I owe back property tax on my Henderson house?

Pay them off at or before closing. Bills left unpaid past January 1 move to the County Clerk and grow by 1% a month plus penalties, and the property stays under a lien. The Clerk's Office at 20 N Main Street can quote a payoff.

Can I sell a Henderson house with open Code Enforcement violations?

Yes. Unpaid fines and abatement costs can become a city lien that outranks earlier private liens but not tax liens, and the total is paid from the sale money. Phone Code Enforcement at (270) 831-1277 for the file before pricing the house.

Do I need to make repairs before selling a Henderson home?

No. A buyer who purchases the house unrepaired takes the work on, while a retail buyer may ask for fixes after inspection. Collect contractor quotes before choosing, since a big repair bill takes a large share of a price near $160,100.

Selling in Paducah

Paducah sits where the Tennessee River meets the Ohio River, roughly halfway between St. Louis and Nashville, and McCracken County runs its government from here. No other Jackson Purchase city is bigger, and the metro area held 103,481 people in 2020. The city covers about 20 square miles of land.

Steamboat repair yards and the Illinois Central shops, completed in 1927, built the older neighborhoods that many sellers now own. A house here is often tied to river history, which shows up in how buyers look at flood maps and old brick.

Ownership and carrying costs

The July 2025 estimate is 26,730 people living in 11,741 households of about 2.19 people each. Homeowners hold 55.0 percent of those households, which leaves a lot of rental stock in town.

  • Typical home value, 2020 through 2024 data: $165,300.

With values in that range, a roof or foundation bill can eat a big slice of the equity. Sellers in that spot often prefer a buyer who needs no lender inspection.

Flood zones and the floodwall

The river's biggest test came in 1937. The Ohio crested at 60.8 feet on February 2, well past the 50 foot flood stage, and about 27,000 residents left their homes for nearly three weeks. Congress then directed the Corps of Engineers to build the floodwall that guards downtown.

Paducah joined FEMA's flood insurance program and, under Chapter 50 of its code, controls building inside Special Flood Hazard Areas. Sixteen flood map panels cover the city. Anyone developing in a hazard area needs a permit application with a $100 fee, plans from a Kentucky registered engineer or architect, and a FEMA Elevation Certificate. Insurers use that same certificate to price a policy, so a buyer's insurance agent may ask for it. Call the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 to learn whether an address sits in a mapped zone.

Historic zones, permits and liens

Lower Town is the oldest neighborhood. Most of its buildings went up after the Civil War, and the Artist Relocation Program has offered incentives for artists to buy and restore homes there since August 2000. A twenty block stretch of downtown is a listed historic district.

  • In the H-1 and H-2 historic zones, exterior changes that show from the street need a Certificate of Appropriateness.
  • Tearing down a structure inside the Demolition Control Zone needs a demolition control permit, with the Planning Director, Chief Building Inspector and a historic commission chair signing off.
  • New or heavily renovated buildings need a final inspection before anyone moves in.
  • The Building Division at 270-444-8690 can confirm whether liens or fines are attached to a property address.

Make that call before choosing an asking price, because an open fine or unpermitted work can slow a closing.

Schools, roads and weather

Paducah Public Schools serves part of the city, and other addresses belong to McCracken County Public Schools. Check which district a house is zoned for before you advertise it. Interstate 24 runs east to Nashville and west toward St. Louis, with a business loop through downtown, and Interstate 69 curves around the east side.

Summers are hot and damp, with roughly 50 inches of annual precipitation and the odd tornado outbreak. Expect buyers to ask about roof age and drainage.

Property tax billing and delinquency

Kentucky fixes real estate values on January 1 each year, and the county's Property Valuation Administrator sets them. That office neither sets rates nor takes payment. Bills become payable at the Sheriff's office on November 1, and paying in full on or before that date trims 2 percent. From November 2 to December 31 the face amount is due. The Sheriff keeps open bills until April 15. Each year the roll opens for public review in early May and stays open 13 days (KRS 133.045). If the conference fails, file with the Clerk, and a three person local panel rules. Anyone still unhappy can go on to the state's Board of Tax Appeals.

Owners 65 and over, or totally disabled, can apply to the PVA for the homestead or disability exemption.

Some of it is. The city maps Special Flood Hazard Areas on 16 FEMA map panels, and the Engineering Department at 270-444-8511 can tell you whether a specific address falls inside one. A mapped address can mean a buyer needs flood insurance, and an elevation certificate helps price that policy.

Which office collects Paducah's property tax bill?

Current bills are paid to the McCracken County Sheriff from November 1. The County Clerk takes over bills still open after April 15. Values come from the PVA, which handles no payments.

What if I still owe taxes when I sell?

Open taxes become a lien at the County Clerk, and the closing agent normally pays that lien from your sale proceeds. The late charge steps up twice after year end, and the Clerk adds 1 percent a month once it holds the bill. Request a payoff amount from the Sheriff or Clerk ahead of closing day.

Does tearing down an old building in Paducah take a permit?

Fifty cents for each $500 of price. The clerk takes it when the deed goes on record, and KRS 142.050 exempts foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers.
